lesson.title: The social contract

lead.text: To see what a government is for, imagine living without one. There are no police, no courts, and no one with the power to make rules and enforce them. Philosophers call this the state of nature. It is a thought experiment and not a claim about history. The point is to ask what people would be like, and what they would need, if nothing but themselves stood between them and one another.

Thomas Hobbes, writing during the English Civil War, pictured it darkly. People are roughly equal in strength, in the sense that even the weakest can kill the strongest by cunning or by teaming up with others. Each wants to stay safe, so each fears the rest and may strike first. Competition, fear and pride push everyone towards what Hobbes called a war of all against all.

afterFigure.text: That picture explains his answer to the question of obedience. If the alternative is endless war, any sensible person would give up the freedom to harm others and obey a single ruler, called a sovereign, who is strong enough to keep the peace. Each person makes that deal because every other person does. The agreement is the social contract, and Hobbes thought the sovereign's power should be nearly complete, because only complete power could end the war.

premises.text: Without a common power, each person may do whatever preserves himself.
Even the weakest can kill the strongest, by plot or alliance.
Competition, fear and pride make conflict likely.

conclusion.text: Without a sovereign, life is a war of all against all.

premises.text: In the state of nature a law of nature already forbids harming others.
People leave it only to secure their lives, liberties and property.

conclusion.text: Government is legitimate only by consent, and only within those limits.

lead.text: The picture you have just read ends in a famous line about how bad life without a government would be.

reveal.text: That is Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651), describing life without a common power.

lead.text: John Locke, writing a generation later, drew a very different picture. In his state of nature people are not at war. They live under a law of nature, a moral law that binds everyone and forbids harming another person's life, liberty or property. The trouble is that nobody is in charge of applying it. People judge their own quarrels, and people favour themselves.

So Locke's people agree to form a government, but their reason is milder than Hobbes's. They want a neutral judge to protect rights they already have. Because they set the government up, its power rests on their consent, their agreement to be governed. Consent also limits it. A government that threatens the lives, liberty and property it was formed to protect has gone beyond the agreement, and the people may replace it.

afterFigure.text: The two pictures agree that government comes from an agreement. They disagree about why people make it and about how far a ruler's power may reach.

steps.headline: Choosing rules without knowing your place

lead.text: The contract tradition returned in the twentieth century with a new question: what would the basic rules of a fair society be? John Rawls proposed a test. Imagine that you must choose the rules for your society before you know where you will stand in it. You do not know whether you will be rich or poor, or what talents you will have. Rawls called the screen that hides all this the veil of ignorance.

A familiar case shows why it helps. When one child cuts a cake and another chooses a slice first, the cutter has every reason to cut evenly, because the cutter does not know which slice will be left. The veil works the same way on a whole society. A rule that favours the rich only looks attractive to someone who knows they are rich, and the veil takes that knowledge away.
Behind the veil you would pick an arrangement that you could live with in whatever place you ended up. The next question tries that on a small scale.
Try the veil with sweets. You choose how to split them, but you do not choose which pile you receive.

reveal.text: Equal piles make the smallest pile as large as it can be. Choosing as if you might be anyone leans towards fairness.

lead.text: Rawls and his critics disagreed about how a person behind the veil should choose. To see the choice, picture a society as three equal groups: a lowest third, a middle third and a top third. A society is described by the income each third receives. You will land in one of the groups, and you do not know which.

One rule is to go by the average. If you are equally likely to land in any group, your expected income is the three incomes added and divided by three, and you choose the society where that is highest. It is the same weighing as in the lesson on consequences. The other rule is maximin, short for maximum minimum: look at the worst position in each society and choose the society whose worst position is best. Rawls argued that when you cannot say how likely each position is, maximin is the prudent rule.

afterFigure.text: In the picture, both societies average 30, so the average rule cannot separate them. The worst-off group gets 20 in P and 12 in Q, so maximin chooses P.

lead.text: Society A pays its three equal groups different incomes. Work out the income you can expect behind the veil.

reveal.text: You averaged the three incomes. Society B's average comes to 30, so on averages alone A looks better.

steps.headline: Compare society A (10, 40, 70) with society C (20, 45, 95) by the average and by maximin.

workedSteps.text: Averages: A is 120 ÷ 3 = 40. C is 160 ÷ 3, about 53.
Worst positions: A pays its lowest group 10 and C pays 20.
C wins on both rules, so there is no dilemma between them here.

lead.text: Maximin looks only at each society's worst position. Compare the lowest income in each society.

reveal.text: B's worst-off group gets 25 and A's gets 10, so maximin picks B even though A has the higher average.

steps.headline: Unequal groups and the difference principle

lead.text: Real societies do not split into equal thirds. Suppose a quarter of the people are in one position and three quarters in another. The average then has to give each income its share of the people: multiply each income by the fraction of people who receive it, and add. The result is a weighted average.

In the picture, Society X pays 20 to the first quarter and 60 to the other three quarters, so its average is 0.25 × 20 + 0.75 × 60 = 50. Society Y pays 28 and 44, which averages 40. On the average rule X wins. Maximin prefers Y, because its worst-off group gets 28 against 20.

afterFigure.text: Maximin ignores the shares. It would choose Y even if the worst-off group were a tiny fraction of the people, and this is the strongest objection to it. John Harsanyi and others argued that a rational chooser should maximise expected utility, which is the average. Rawls turned his side into a rule for real institutions, the difference principle: social and economic inequalities are allowed only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.

lead.text: Real groups differ in size. In Society D a quarter of the people are in one position and three quarters in another.

reveal.text: Maximin ignores the shares and looks only at the worst position, which is the strongest objection to it.

lesson.orientation: Compare Hobbes's and Locke's social contracts, then choose principles behind Rawls's veil of ignorance with maximin and averages.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Think about the rules you followed today without being asked. You stopped at a red light and paid for what you bought. Behind all of them stands a government that can punish you if you do not. Most of us accept that arrangement so completely that we rarely ask why we should.

Some philosophers asked it seriously. If nobody has a natural right to rule you, what could give a government that right? Their answer was an agreement made among free people who see that life is better under rules. Different thinkers pictured the agreement differently, and their pictures led to very different governments.

This lesson begins with life before any government and with two of those pictures. It then turns to a thought experiment about a society's basic rules, which asks you to choose them without knowing where in the society you would end up. You test two ways of choosing with numbers, and find that they can point in different directions.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say why Hobbes and Locke think we should obey a government, and compare two ways of choosing fair rules.

recap.keyIdea: Contract theories ask what people would agree to. Behind the veil, averages and maximin can choose differently.

blocks.text: You averaged incomes for three societies and found where the average and the worst case agree and where they part. You also saw how Hobbes and Locke answer the question of why we obey.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course. Come back to any idea after a delay to see how much has stayed with you.

questions.prompt: Who wrote that, without a common power, the life of man would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'?
hints: He wrote Leviathan during the English Civil War.
questions.onCorrect: Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651), describing life without a common power.

misconceptions.feedback: That philosopher belongs to the story, but is not the author of this line. Think of the author of Leviathan.

questions.prompt: Society A pays its three equal-sized groups 10, 40 and 70 income units. If you are equally likely to land in any group, what is your expected income in A?
hints: Each group has probability one third.
Add the three incomes.
Divide by the number of groups.
questions.onCorrect: 40 income units: the three incomes added and divided by three.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the top group's income. Add all three incomes and divide.
That is the total. Divide by the number of groups.

questions.prompt: Behind the veil you choose between society A (10, 40, 70) and society B (25, 30, 35), three equal groups each. Which society does the maximin rule choose? Answer A or B.
hints: Maximin looks only at each society's worst position.
Compare the lowest income in each society.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Society B: its worst-off group receives 25, against 10 in A.

questions.onCorrect: Society B: its worst-off group gets more than A's, and maximin looks only at the worst position.

misconceptions.feedback: Maximin ignores the average. Compare the lowest income in each society.

questions.prompt: In society D, a quarter of people receive 30 income units and three quarters receive 50. What is the average income?
hints: Weight each income by the share of people who receive it.
Multiply 30 by a quarter and 50 by three quarters.
Add the two weighted amounts.
questions.onCorrect: 45 income units: each income weighted by the share of people who receive it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average if the groups were equal. Weight each income by its share.
That is the two incomes added. Weight each by its share of the people.

questions.prompt: Locke held that legitimate political power rests on the ___ of the governed. Fill the gap with one word.
hints: Locke's citizens make themselves members of a society by their own act.
The word for agreeing to something.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Consent: people leave the state of nature by agreeing to form a political society.

questions.onCorrect: Consent: people leave the state of nature by agreeing to form a political society.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of Locke's picture, but not what legitimacy rests on. Think of agreeing to something.

questions.prompt: Rawls's difference principle permits social and economic inequalities only when:
hints: The principle is the institutional cousin of maximin.

acceptedIdeas: They work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inequalities must benefit the least advantaged, and attach to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity.

choices.label: They work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged
Everyone receives exactly the same income

questions.onCorrect: Inequalities must work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, the cousin of maximin.

misconceptions.feedback: Rawls does not require equal incomes. Inequalities are allowed under a condition.
Raising the average is the utilitarian aim. The difference principle asks about the least advantaged.

questions.prompt: You must split 12 sweets into three piles, and you will be handed whichever pile turns out smallest. How many sweets should the smallest pile hold, to give yourself the most?
hints: Whatever piles you make, you receive the smallest one.
What happens to the smallest pile if you make the piles unequal?
Share the 12 sweets so that the smallest pile is as large as it can be.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal piles of 4 make the smallest pile as large as possible: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: Equal piles give you the best worst case. Choosing as if you might be anyone leans towards fairness.

misconceptions.feedback: Making the piles unequal only shrinks the one you will receive. Look for the largest smallest pile.
That is the whole stock. There are three piles to fill.

questions.prompt: Why would people in Hobbes's state of nature accept a sovereign?
hints: Think of what life is like with no common power.

acceptedIdeas: To escape a war of all against all
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To escape a war of all against all

choices.label: To escape a war of all against all
Because a law of nature already forbids harm

questions.onCorrect: Without a sovereign, fear and competition lead to conflict. Obedience is the way out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Locke's state of nature. Hobbes thought nothing restrains people without a common power.
Kindness plays no part. Think of what life is like with no common power.

questions.prompt: Behind the veil, what do you know?
hints: The veil hides your place in society.

acceptedIdeas: How society is arranged, but not which position is yours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How society is arranged, but not which position is yours

choices.label: How society is arranged, but not which position is yours

questions.onCorrect: You can compare arrangements, but you cannot tilt them towards your own position.

misconceptions.feedback: Income is part of your place in society, which the veil hides.
Talents are part of what the veil hides along with class and your view of the good.

questions.prompt: Why is there no dilemma between A and C?
hints: Compare both numbers for each society.

acceptedIdeas: C does better on the average and for the worst-off.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: C does better on the average and for the worst-off.

choices.label: C does better on the average and for the worst-off.

questions.onCorrect: When one society wins on both rules, the choice is easy. The rules matter only when they disagree.

misconceptions.feedback: Both societies have three groups. Compare both numbers for each society.
Averages are one of the two rules in play. Compare both numbers for each society.

questions.prompt: Society F pays three equal groups 15, 30 and 60. Society G pays them 20, 25 and 30. By how many units does F's average exceed G's?
hints: Find each society's total, then divide by the number of groups.
Find F's average and G's average separately.
Subtract G's average from F's.
questions.onCorrect: F's average is higher by ten units, though its worst-off group does worse. The rules can pull apart.

misconceptions.feedback: That is F's average. The question asks for the gap between the two averages.
That is G's average. The question asks for the gap between the two averages.
